items.title: Abbey Lincoln — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: It's a rare woman, like Melba Liston, who comes to the music for the music.

ctx.x: -- you're talking about feminists objecting to that. What about this more sort of interpretation of the music now from different perspectives, of women's history in jazz from more feminists' perspective?

Women don't have a history in jazz. That's just a lot of garbage the feminists have brought to us. Listen, women have the same history in jazz as they do in classical music. Does she -- is she the composer? Does she conduct the orchestra? She sings, just like they do in this form. If we depended on women to bring music, we'd be in trouble. They don't bring music. They bring babies. They become famous being married to a man. It's a rare woman, like Melba Liston, who comes to the music for the music. Rare. Hazel…
Why do you think that is?

items.title: Melba Liston — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Oh, she’s fine. I write for her now and then.

ctx.x: I guess okay. I didn’t have no problem ever. Not with the singers and the instrumentalists that I wrote for. Maybe a bandperson now and then, but he would come in right quick. Not in the last 20 years. I haven’t had none of that.
Oh, she’s fine. I write for her now and then.
